title: Simple Fraction Sums
keyIdea: When two fractions have the same denominator, the parts are the same size, so you add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5 and 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8. Adding the denominators as well (4/10) is wrong, because the parts do not change size. When the numerator equals the denominator, as in 5/5, the fraction is one whole.

kid: A fraction counts equal parts. In 2/5 the bottom number, 5, is the denominator. It tells you the whole is cut into 5 equal parts, called fifths. The top number, 2, is the numerator. It counts how many parts you have.
Add 2 fifths and 2 fifths. You get 4 fifths. The parts are still fifths, so 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5. Add the numerators. Keep the denominator the same.
Take away works the same way. You have 6 eighths and take away 3 eighths. 3 eighths are left, so 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8. The parts are still eighths.
Five fifths fill the whole bar. So 5/5 is one whole. If you have 3/5, you need 2/5 more to make 1. On a number line, each hop of 1/7 moves you one seventh.
adult: England's Year 3 programme asks pupils to 'add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole', for example 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7. The US standard 4.NF.B.3a describes the same idea: adding and subtracting fractions means joining and separating parts that refer to the same whole. In the US this comes in Grade 4.

The key idea is the unit. A fifth is a unit, just like a one or a ten. Four fifths is four of that unit, so adding fifths is like counting. The denominator names the unit and does not change when you add or take away.

Common mistakes: adding the denominators as well as the numerators (2/5 + 2/5 = 4/10), taking away the denominators to get answers like 3/0, and multiplying the numerators. A quick check helps: 4/10 is less than a half, but 2/5 + 2/5 must be more than 2/5 on its own.

In the lab your child slides fifths from two bars into one bar, answers sums while a wrong 'add the bottoms' answer is drawn to scale, crosses out parts to subtract, fills a bar to make one whole, and hops in sevenths along a number line from 0 to 1.

familyTip: Cut a pizza, a pancake or a sheet of paper into 8 equal slices. Each eat or move some slices and say the sum out loud: 3 eighths and 2 eighths make 5 eighths. Ask: did the slices get smaller when we added? Then ask how many more eighths would make the whole.

visual.caption: Two bars the same length, both cut into fifths. 2/5 is shaded on one and 4/5 on the other: two more fifths, same-size parts.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: slide fifths into one bar, add sevenths and eighths, cross out parts to subtract, fill to one whole and hop in sevenths.

practice.hint: The parts are all ninths. Add the numerators and keep the denominator.
practice.explain: {a} ninths + {b} ninths = {=a+b} ninths, so {a}/9 + {b}/9 = {=a+b}/9. The denominator stays 9.

practice.hint: Take away the numerators. The parts are still tenths.
practice.explain: {=a+b} tenths take away {b} tenths leaves {a} tenths, so the answer is {a}/10.

practice.prompt: {a}/8 + ?/8 = 1 whole. What is the missing numerator?
practice.hint: One whole cut into eighths is 8/8. How many more eighths do you need?
practice.explain: One whole is 8/8. You have {a}/8, so you need {=8-a} more eighths: {a}/8 + {=8-a}/8 = 8/8 = 1.

practice.hint: Are the parts still fifths after you add them?
practice.explain: 2 fifths + 2 fifths = 4 fifths, so 4/5. 4/10 adds the denominators too, but the parts did not get smaller.

pool.hint: Twelfths plus twelfths gives twelfths. Add only the numerators.
pool.explain: {a} twelfths + {b} twelfths = {=a+b} twelfths, so the answer is {=a+b}/12.

pool.prompt: Mia walks {a}/10 of a mile before lunch and {b}/10 of a mile after lunch. How many tenths of a mile does she walk in all?
pool.hint: Both parts are tenths of a mile, so add the numerators.
pool.explain: {a} tenths + {b} tenths = {=a+b} tenths, so she walks {=a+b}/10 of a mile.

pool.hint: Take away the numerators. What size are the parts that are left?
pool.explain: 7 eighths − 2 eighths = 5 eighths, so 5/8. 5/0 takes away the denominators, and 9/8 adds instead.

pool.prompt: Which fraction is equal to one whole?
pool.hint: One whole has every part. Look for the same numerator and denominator.
pool.explain: 6/6 is all 6 sixths, so it is one whole. 1/6 is one part and 6/12 is only half.

pool.prompt: Leo says 3/7 + 2/7 = 5/14. What did he do wrong?
pool.hint: Did the parts change size when he added them?
pool.explain: He added the denominators. The parts are still sevenths, so 3/7 + 2/7 = 5/7.

pool.prompt: A cake is cut into 4 equal slices. You eat 1/4. How much is left?
pool.hint: The whole cake is 4/4. Take away the slice you ate.
pool.explain: 4/4 − 1/4 = 3/4. Three quarters of the cake is left.

pool.prompt: A frog starts at 2/7 on a number line and hops 3/7 to the right. Where does it land?
pool.hint: Each hop of 1/7 moves one step. Count on 3 sevenths from 2/7.
pool.explain: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7. Counting on in sevenths is like counting on in ones.

pool.hint: Add the numerators: 1 + 1 + 1. Keep the denominator.
pool.explain: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 3/3, which is one whole. 3/9 adds the denominators too.
